CORS
Last reviewed 2026-10-04 · Jump to reference

Objective. Explain what a successful CORS check does and does not establish, find the two configurations that hand a response to any site, and test a preflight that refuses what it should.

Before you start. You should be able to read an HTTP request and a Python function. An origin is the scheme, host and port of a URL taken together. CORS is the mechanism by which a server tells a browser that a response may be handed to a page from another origin. It is enforced by the browser, not by the server.

Learn
1. The attack

ExampleHotels runs an internal reporting API at api.examplehotels.example. It authenticates with a session cookie. A partner dashboard on app.examplehotels.example needed to call it from the browser, so a developer added the two headers that made the error go away: echo back whatever Origin arrived, and allow credentials. These companies are fictional. The configuration is not.

An attacker publishes a page on booking-rewards.example. A logged-in employee visits it. The page runs a fetch with credentials included. The browser attaches the cookie, because that is what including credentials means. The server echoes Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://booking-rewards.example and Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true. The browser's CORS check passes, and the attacker's JavaScript reads the report. This is an illustration, not a command.

The third row is the one people are surprised by, and it is covered in section 5.
2. Why it works

The browser's gate is the CORS check, and the Fetch Standard defines it in eight steps. Condensed: if there is no Access-Control-Allow-Origin header, fail. If it is * and the request did not include credentials, succeed. Otherwise it must equal the request's serialised origin exactly. If credentials were included, Access-Control-Allow-Credentials must also be the byte string true.

A server that echoes the Origin header passes step 4 by construction. There is nothing left to compare. The check is not asking whether this origin is trusted; it is asking whether the server named it, and an echoing server names every origin that asks.

The standard is explicit about why the protocol has to be opt-in: "It needs to be an opt-in mechanism to prevent leaking data from responses behind a firewall (intranets). Additionally, for requests including credentials it needs to be opt-in to prevent leaking potentially-sensitive data." On credentials specifically it says that "both sharing responses and allowing requests with credentials is rather unsafe, and extreme care has to be taken to avoid the confused deputy problem" (Fetch Standard sections 3.3 and 3.3.5).

Two further reasons this configuration survives review. First, Origin is not an authentication mechanism. A browser sets it and will not let a page forge it, but curl sets whatever it is told to, so the header means something only inside a browser. Second, the preflight is widely read as an authorisation step. It is not. The standard describes it as a request "that checks to see if the CORS protocol is understood".
3. The control

In order:

  1. Keep a list of exact serialised origins. Compare the incoming Origin against it byte for byte. A serialised origin has no trailing slash and no path, so https://app.examplehotels.example/ never matches.
  2. Never build the header from the request. If the origin is on the list, send that origin. If it is not, send no Access-Control-Allow-Origin at all. Omitting the header is how the protocol says no.
  3. Never pair * with credentials. The standard forbids it, and so does every browser: with credentials included, * fails the check. The same applies to * in Access-Control-Allow-Methods, Access-Control-Allow-Headers and Access-Control-Expose-Headers.
  4. Send Vary: Origin whenever the response depends on the request's origin, so a shared cache cannot serve one origin's allowed response to another.
  5. Name Authorization explicitly in Access-Control-Allow-Headers. It is the one CORS non-wildcard request-header name, so * does not cover it, and neither does a cached preflight entry stored as *.
  6. Put a bound on Access-Control-Max-Age. It defaults to 5 seconds, browsers cap it, and a long value delays the moment a policy change takes effect.
  7. Keep authorisation on the server. CORS decides who may read a response. It never decides who may cause one.

4. Defaults and when to change them

Access-Control-Max-Age. Absent or unparsable, it is 5 seconds. Browsers also clamp it to their own ceiling, so a value of 86400 does not mean a day. Short values cost a preflight on almost every request; long values mean a tightened policy keeps being ignored until the cache expires. Set it deliberately and know your ceiling.

Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *. For genuinely public data this is correct, not sloppy, and the standard says so plainly in a background section it marks as informative only. Its test is worth memorising: "if a resource cannot be accessed from a random device connected to the web using curl and wget the aforementioned header is not to be included. If it can be accessed however, it is perfectly fine to do so." The failure case it names is data "protected through IP authentication or a firewall", where CORS is unsafe, because the browser of someone inside the perimeter becomes the way in.

The safelist thresholds. A request avoids a preflight only if its method is GET, HEAD or POST and every header is CORS-safelisted. Two limits decide that: no single safelisted value may exceed 128 bytes, and the safelisted values together may not exceed 1024 bytes. Cross either and the request preflights, which is a behaviour change you did not configure and will see as a latency change.

Reflecting the origin. There is one defensible version: reflect only after checking the origin against a list, which is what sending the matched origin back amounts to. There is no defensible version that skips the check.
5. What it proves, and what it doesn't

Proves: that the server named this origin in a response header, and, when credentials were included, that it also said credentials may be shared. That is the whole of it.

Doesn't prove: anything about who the user is, or whether the operation was allowed. The CORS check runs in the browser after the response arrives.

Doesn't stop the request. This is the row in the table above that catches people. A cross-origin POST with a safelisted content type is sent with no preflight at all, the server authenticates the cookie and does the work, and the browser then withholds the response. The write happened. Preventing unwanted cross-origin writes is the job of anti-forgery tokens and same-site cookies, not CORS.

Doesn't apply outside a browser. A server-to-server client sets Origin to whatever it likes, or omits it. Treating the header as an access control decision is treating attacker input as a credential.

Doesn't survive a wildcard in the wrong place. A preflight that answers Access-Control-Allow-Headers: * has not allowed Authorization, and a request carrying it will fail. That is a correctness trap more often than a security one, but it is the reason a working integration breaks when someone adds a bearer token.
6. Prove it

A working configuration must refuse every one of these. If any is accepted, the control is broken:

  • A request from an origin that is not on the list gets no Access-Control-Allow-Origin header at all.
  • A request from an origin that is a prefix or suffix of an allowed one, such as https://app.examplehotels.example.evil.example, is refused.
  • The same host over http instead of https is refused.
  • An allowed origin with a trailing slash is refused, which proves the comparison is on the serialised form.
  • No response that allows credentials ever carries Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *.
  • Every response whose headers depend on the request's origin carries Vary: Origin.
  • A preflight for a method the endpoint does not support is answered without that method, and the real request never follows.
  • A request carrying Authorization fails against a preflight that answers only Access-Control-Allow-Headers: *, and succeeds when the header is named.
  • A preflight answered with a redirect or a 500 fails, rather than being treated as permissive.
  • All of the above are tests in the build, asserted against the response headers rather than checked by hand in a browser console.

Three results are worth sitting with. Under a forgiving parser that lets the last valid value win, the same request would skip the preflight while a server reading the first value still treats the body as JSON. The strictness is the defence.

Checks 23 to 28 show the aggregate limit doing something invisible. Eight safelisted headers of exactly 128 bytes total exactly 1024, which is not over 1024, so a GET still goes straight out. A ninth header tips the total to 1152 and every safelisted name turns unsafe at once, so the same GET now preflights.

Checks 44 and 45 are the Authorization trap from section 5, and checks 58 and 59 show the same rule inside the preflight cache: an entry stored as * matches Content-Type and never matches Authorization.
8. Check your understanding

Your API echoes the Origin header back in Access-Control-Allow-Origin and sets Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true. Which origins can read the response?

All of them. The CORS check compares the header against the request's own origin, so echoing makes step 4 compare a value with itself and it can never fail. The configuration is equivalent to publishing every authenticated response to any site a logged-in user happens to visit.

A cross-origin POST was blocked by CORS. Did the server process it?

Almost certainly yes. If the content type was safelisted there was no preflight, so the request went straight out, the cookie went with it, and the server did the work. The browser then refused to hand the response to the page. What CORS blocked was the reading, not the writing. Use anti-forgery tokens and SameSite cookies for the writing.

You add a bearer token to a working cross-origin integration and it starts failing the preflight, even though the server answers Access-Control-Allow-Headers: *. Why?

Authorization is the one CORS non-wildcard request-header name, so * does not cover it. The server has to name it. The same rule applies to the preflight cache, so an entry previously stored as * will not match it either.

Is Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * a finding?

Only with context. For data that anyone could already fetch with curl, it is the correct header and the standard says so. It is unsafe in exactly one shape: when the resource is protected by where the caller is rather than by who they are, such as an IP allowlist or a firewall, because then a browser inside the perimeter becomes the route in. Ask what protects the resource before writing the finding.

attrs.data-correct-feedback: Correct. The check compares Access-Control-Allow-Origin against the request's own origin, so a server that echoes it always matches, and every origin is allowed.
attrs.data-incorrect-feedback: Not quite. The preflight, HTTPS and the cookie are all real, and none of them changes the fact that an echoed origin always equals the origin it was echoed from. The browser attaches the cookie to the attacker page's request too.

Quick check

Echoing the origin

An API returns Access-Control-Allow-Origin set to whatever arrived in Origin, plus Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true. What limits which sites can read authenticated responses?

Exercises

Change one thing and predict the output

Each exercise edits one place in labs/cors_lab.py and asks what the run prints. The answers are the real output of each variant. One variant changes nothing, and its answer carries the measurement from a request the lab does not make.

1. The allowlist is matched by prefix

In allowlist_server, replace the membership test with a prefix test. ALLOWED_ORIGINS stays as it is:

if request_origin.startswith(ALLOWED_ORIGINS):
Which checks change?

Every option, and why
  • Check 66 still prints failure. https://booking-rewards.example does not begin with either listed origin, so a prefix test refuses it too. An unrelated origin is the test a loosened comparison still passes.
  • The lab carries a lookalike origin for exactly this edit, so the run does not stay clean. It exits 1.
  • Correct. Exit 1, two failures. Check 70 goes from ['success', 'success', 'failure', 'failure', 'failure'] to ['success', 'success', 'failure', 'success', 'failure'], and in check 71 the fourth entry goes from None to 'https://app.examplehotels.example.evil.example'. That origin begins with an allowed one, so the server sends it back with credentials allowed, and anyone can register a host of that shape. Checks 65 to 68 print the same as before, which is why check cors-01 in the Reference layer asks for a lookalike as well as a disallowed origin.
  • The fifth origin is http://app.examplehotels.example. It differs from the listed origin inside the scheme, before the host starts, so it is not a prefix match and its entry in checks 70 and 71 does not move.

2. The reflecting server sends a wildcard instead

Someone reads that echoing the origin is unsafe and changes reflecting_server to stop echoing. In the pair it returns for Access-Control-Allow-Origin, replace request_origin with the string "*". The Access-Control-Allow-Credentials pair stays "true".

What does the run print differently?

Every option, and why
  • A wildcard succeeds only when credentials were not included. Checks 62, 63 and 69 all call cors_check with "include", so the wildcard line is skipped and * is then compared with the origin as a plain string. It equals none of them.
  • The check has no idea which origin is the real app. It compares one string with another, and * differs from https://app.examplehotels.example just as it differs from the attacker's origin.
  • Check 69 runs against reflecting_server, which has no list. ALLOWED_ORIGINS is read only by allowlist_server, and check 70 is the one that uses it.
  • Correct. Exit 1, four failures. Checks 62 and 63 go from success to failure, check 64 goes from https://booking-rewards.example to *, and check 69 goes from five times success to five times failure. The attacker is locked out, and so is the real dashboard, because a wildcard with credentials included fails the check for every origin. That is the same outcome as check 38 in Part B. The edit closes the hole by breaking the integration, which is not a fix anyone keeps. Check cors-02 in the Reference layer is the assertion that catches this pairing before it ships.

3. The non-wildcard name rule is removed from the preflight

In preflight_fetch, delete the whole for name, _ in headers: loop, the one that returns is a non-wildcard name and was not listed. The loop after it, over unsafe_request_header_names(headers), stays.

What does the run print differently?

Every option, and why
  • Not in this lab. Check 44 sends its request with credentials included, and the loop that is left honours * in Access-Control-Allow-Headers only when credentials are not included. Authorization is an unsafe name that was not listed, so the preflight is still refused.
  • Correct. Exit 1, one failure: check 45 goes from Authorization is a non-wildcard name and was not listed to header authorization is not allowed by the preflight. Check 44 is unchanged. The request is still refused, by a different rule, and only because this request includes credentials. Measured on a preflight the lab does not make, with credentials omitted, Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *, Access-Control-Allow-Methods: PATCH and Access-Control-Allow-Headers: *, for the same request carrying Authorization: as published the answer is network error with the non-wildcard reason, and with the loop deleted it is ok with a max age of 5. Check cors-07 in the Reference layer exists because the wildcard never covers this one name, with or without credentials.
  • The lab compares the reason in check 45 as well as the outcome in check 44, so a change of reason fails the run even though the verdict is the same.
  • Check 59 is answered by PreflightCache.header_match, which carries its own non-wildcard comparison. This edit does not touch it, and check 59 still prints False.

4. Vary is sent only when the origin is refused

In allowlist_server, remove the ("Vary", "Origin") pair from the list returned for an allowed origin. The last line of the function, which returns Vary alone for every other origin, stays.

What does the run print differently?

Every option, and why
  • Correct. Exit 0, 84 of 84 lines identical. The only place the lab reads Vary is check 68, and that reads the response to the attacker, which this edit leaves alone. Measured on a lookup the lab does not make, the Vary header on the response to https://app.examplehotels.example: as published it is Origin, and with the pair removed it is None. The allowed response is the one that names an origin and allows credentials, so it is the one a shared cache must not serve to a different origin, and it is now the one with nothing telling the cache so. Check cors-05 in the Reference layer says wherever the response depends on the origin, which is both branches.
  • That is the other branch. Removing Vary from the refusal changes check 68 from Origin to None and the run exits 1. This edit removes it from the allowed response, which check 68 never sees.
  • cors_check reads Access-Control-Allow-Origin and Access-Control-Allow-Credentials and nothing else. Vary is an instruction to caches, and the check never looks at it.
  • Check 71 prints only the Access-Control-Allow-Origin value sent to each of the five origins. Those values are unchanged.

Reference
Controls
Standard backed by a cited specification. Baseline this project's default, with reasoning above. Option valid depending on the threat model.

• StandardThe CORS check reads Access-Control-Allow-Origin, fails if it is absent, succeeds on * only when credentials were not included, otherwise requires it to equal the request's byte-serialised origin, and when credentials were included additionally requires Access-Control-Allow-Credentials to be true. Fetch Standard section 4.10.
  • StandardAccess-Control-Allow-Credentials = %s"true" ; case-sensitive. True does not satisfy it. Fetch Standard section 3.3.4.
  • StandardWith credentials mode include, Access-Control-Allow-Origin cannot be *, and Access-Control-Expose-Headers, Access-Control-Allow-Methods and Access-Control-Allow-Headers can only use * when credentials mode is not include. Fetch Standard section 3.3.5.
  • StandardA serialised origin has no trailing slash, its scheme and domain are lower case ASCII without percent encoding, and this definition "supplants the definition in The Web Origin Concept". Fetch Standard section 3.2, and the table in section 3.3.5 for the trailing slash.
  • StandardAuthorization is the CORS non-wildcard request-header name, so Access-Control-Allow-Headers: * does not cover it, and a cached preflight entry stored as * does not match it. Fetch Standard sections 2.2.2, 4.8 and 4.9.
  • StandardA request avoids a preflight only for a CORS-safelisted method, GET, HEAD or POST, with every header CORS-safelisted: no single safelisted value over 128 bytes, and the safelisted values together not over 1024 bytes. Fetch Standard sections 2.2.1 and 2.2.2 for the definitions, and 4.1 for the preflight condition.
  • StandardA safelisted Content-Type must parse to application/x-www-form-urlencoded, multipart/form-data or text/plain, judged per header rather than through a forgiving extractor, so a server that reads a different duplicate than the browser judged is the hazard the standard warns about. Fetch Standard section 2.2.2.
  • StandardA successful response to a preflight is restricted to an ok status; Access-Control-Max-Age is 5 seconds by default, and a value greater than an imposed limit is set to that limit. Fetch Standard sections 3.3.3 and 4.8.
  • StandardFour non-safelisted Content-Type values are exempted from preflighting by other specifications: application/csp-report, application/expect-ct-report+json, application/xss-auditor-report and application/ocsp-request. Fetch Standard section 3.3.7.
  • StandardThe standard's informative background section says Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * is safe for a resource that could already be fetched by any device on the web, and that using CORS is unsafe for one protected by IP authentication or a firewall. Fetch Standard, Basic safe CORS protocol setup, under Background reading.
  • BaselineHold an allowlist of exact serialised origins and compare byte for byte. Send the matched origin, or no Access-Control-Allow-Origin header at all.
  • BaselineNever construct the header from the request. Reflecting an unchecked origin allows every origin.
  • BaselineSend Vary: Origin on every response whose headers depend on the request's origin.
  • BaselineSet Access-Control-Max-Age deliberately, knowing the browser ceiling, and treat it as the delay before a tightened policy takes effect.
  • BaselineAssert the CORS response headers in tests, against allowed, disallowed and lookalike origins, rather than confirming the integration works in a browser console.
  • BaselineProtect state-changing endpoints with anti-forgery tokens and SameSite cookies. CORS does not stop the request arriving.
  • OptionServe the browser-facing API from the same origin through a reverse proxy, which removes the cross-origin question rather than configuring it.
  • OptionUse a bearer token in Authorization rather than a cookie, so a cross-origin request carries no credential unless the page deliberately attaches one. Name the header in the preflight response.
Review checklist items
These are collected into the site checklist.

• The allowed origin is never taken from the request Test a disallowed origin and a lookalike such as an allowed host with an extra suffix. Both must come back with no Access-Control-Allow-Origin header.
  • State-changing endpoints are protected independently of CORS A safelisted cross-origin POST is sent with no preflight and the server does the work. Anti-forgery tokens and SameSite cookies are what stop it.
  • Origin comparison is on the serialised form Byte for byte, no trailing slash, scheme and port included. Test the same host over http and with a trailing slash.
  • Vary: Origin is sent wherever the response depends on the origin Otherwise a shared cache can serve one origin's allowed response to another.
  • The Origin header is never used as an authorisation decision A non-browser client sets it freely. It is attacker input outside a browser.
  • Access-Control-Max-Age is set deliberately and bounded It defaults to 5 seconds and browsers clamp it. The value is how long a tightened policy keeps being ignored.
  • Preflight responses are asserted in tests, not confirmed by hand Include a method the endpoint does not support, a request carrying Authorization, and a preflight answered with a redirect.
Sources

• Fetch Standard, WHATWG Living Standard. The text checked is commit snapshot 357bd98, Last Updated 21 September 2026, which was still the current text on 4 October 2026. The snapshot page says not to reference it as authoritative, so the living standard is the reference and the snapshot records what was read. CORS has no RFC; this is the specification.

The server echoes Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://booking-rewards.example and Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true. The browser's CORS check passes, and the attacker's JavaScript reads the report. This is an illustration, not a command.

The third row is the one people are surprised by, and it is covered in section 5.

sections.heading: 2. Why it works
sections.html:
The browser's gate is the CORS check, and the Fetch Standard defines it in eight steps. Condensed: if there is no Access-Control-Allow-Origin header, fail. If it is * and the request did not include credentials, succeed. Otherwise it must equal the request's serialised origin exactly. If credentials were included, Access-Control-Allow-Credentials must also be the byte string true.

A server that echoes the Origin header passes step 4 by construction. There is nothing left to compare. The check is not asking whether this origin is trusted; it is asking whether the server named it, and an echoing server names every origin that asks.

The standard is explicit about why the protocol has to be opt-in: "It needs to be an opt-in mechanism to prevent leaking data from responses behind a firewall (intranets). Additionally, for requests including credentials it needs to be opt-in to prevent leaking potentially-sensitive data." On credentials specifically it says that "both sharing responses and allowing requests with credentials is rather unsafe, and extreme care has to be taken to avoid the confused deputy problem" (Fetch Standard sections 3.3 and 3.3.5).

Two further reasons this configuration survives review. First, Origin is not an authentication mechanism. A browser sets it and will not let a page forge it, but curl sets whatever it is told to, so the header means something only inside a browser. Second, the preflight is widely read as an authorisation step. It is not. The standard describes it as a request "that checks to see if the CORS protocol is understood".

sections.heading: 3. The control
sections.html:
In order:

  1. Keep a list of exact serialised origins. Compare the incoming Origin against it byte for byte. A serialised origin has no trailing slash and no path, so https://app.examplehotels.example/ never matches.
  2. Never build the header from the request. If the origin is on the list, send that origin. If it is not, send no Access-Control-Allow-Origin at all. Omitting the header is how the protocol says no.
  3. Never pair * with credentials. The standard forbids it, and so does every browser: with credentials included, * fails the check. The same applies to * in Access-Control-Allow-Methods, Access-Control-Allow-Headers and Access-Control-Expose-Headers.
  4. Send Vary: Origin whenever the response depends on the request's origin, so a shared cache cannot serve one origin's allowed response to another.
  5. Name Authorization explicitly in Access-Control-Allow-Headers. It is the one CORS non-wildcard request-header name, so * does not cover it, and neither does a cached preflight entry stored as *.
  6. Put a bound on Access-Control-Max-Age. It defaults to 5 seconds, browsers cap it, and a long value delays the moment a policy change takes effect.
  7. Keep authorisation on the server. CORS decides who may read a response. It never decides who may cause one.

sections.heading: 4. Defaults and when to change them
sections.heading_text: 4. Defaults and when to change them
sections.html:
Access-Control-Max-Age. Absent or unparsable, it is 5 seconds. Browsers also clamp it to their own ceiling, so a value of 86400 does not mean a day. Short values cost a preflight on almost every request; long values mean a tightened policy keeps being ignored until the cache expires. Set it deliberately and know your ceiling.

Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *. For genuinely public data this is correct, not sloppy, and the standard says so plainly in a background section it marks as informative only. Its test is worth memorising: "if a resource cannot be accessed from a random device connected to the web using curl and wget the aforementioned header is not to be included. If it can be accessed however, it is perfectly fine to do so." The failure case it names is data "protected through IP authentication or a firewall", where CORS is unsafe, because the browser of someone inside the perimeter becomes the way in.

The safelist thresholds. A request avoids a preflight only if its method is GET, HEAD or POST and every header is CORS-safelisted. Two limits decide that: no single safelisted value may exceed 128 bytes, and the safelisted values together may not exceed 1024 bytes. Cross either and the request preflights, which is a behaviour change you did not configure and will see as a latency change.

Reflecting the origin. There is one defensible version: reflect only after checking the origin against a list, which is what sending the matched origin back amounts to. There is no defensible version that skips the check.

sections.heading: 5. What it proves, and what it doesn't
sections.heading_text: 5. What it proves, and what it doesn't
sections.html:
Proves: that the server named this origin in a response header, and, when credentials were included, that it also said credentials may be shared. That is the whole of it.

Doesn't prove: anything about who the user is, or whether the operation was allowed. The CORS check runs in the browser after the response arrives.

Doesn't stop the request. This is the row in the table above that catches people. A cross-origin POST with a safelisted content type is sent with no preflight at all, the server authenticates the cookie and does the work, and the browser then withholds the response. The write happened. Preventing unwanted cross-origin writes is the job of anti-forgery tokens and same-site cookies, not CORS.

Doesn't apply outside a browser. A server-to-server client sets Origin to whatever it likes, or omits it. Treating the header as an access control decision is treating attacker input as a credential.

Doesn't survive a wildcard in the wrong place. A preflight that answers Access-Control-Allow-Headers: * has not allowed Authorization, and a request carrying it will fail. That is a correctness trap more often than a security one, but it is the reason a working integration breaks when someone adds a bearer token.

sections.heading: 6. Prove it
sections.html:
A working configuration must refuse every one of these. If any is accepted, the control is broken:

  • A request from an origin that is not on the list gets no Access-Control-Allow-Origin header at all.
  • A request from an origin that is a prefix or suffix of an allowed one, such as https://app.examplehotels.example.evil.example, is refused.
  • The same host over http instead of https is refused.
  • An allowed origin with a trailing slash is refused, which proves the comparison is on the serialised form.
  • No response that allows credentials ever carries Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *.
  • Every response whose headers depend on the request's origin carries Vary: Origin.
  • A preflight for a method the endpoint does not support is answered without that method, and the real request never follows.
  • A request carrying Authorization fails against a preflight that answers only Access-Control-Allow-Headers: *, and succeeds when the header is named.
  • A preflight answered with a redirect or a 500 fails, rather than being treated as permissive.
  • All of the above are tests in the build, asserted against the response headers rather than checked by hand in a browser console.

sections.heading: 8. Check your understanding
sections.html:
Your API echoes the Origin header back in Access-Control-Allow-Origin and sets Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true. Which origins can read the response?

All of them. The CORS check compares the header against the request's own origin, so echoing makes step 4 compare a value with itself and it can never fail. The configuration is equivalent to publishing every authenticated response to any site a logged-in user happens to visit.

A cross-origin POST was blocked by CORS. Did the server process it?

Almost certainly yes. If the content type was safelisted there was no preflight, so the request went straight out, the cookie went with it, and the server did the work. The browser then refused to hand the response to the page. What CORS blocked was the reading, not the writing. Use anti-forgery tokens and SameSite cookies for the writing.

You add a bearer token to a working cross-origin integration and it starts failing the preflight, even though the server answers Access-Control-Allow-Headers: *. Why?

Authorization is the one CORS non-wildcard request-header name, so * does not cover it. The server has to name it. The same rule applies to the preflight cache, so an entry previously stored as * will not match it either.

Is Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * a finding?

Only with context. For data that anyone could already fetch with curl, it is the correct header and the standard says so. It is unsafe in exactly one shape: when the resource is protected by where the caller is rather than by who they are, such as an IP allowlist or a firewall, because then a browser inside the perimeter becomes the route in. Ask what protects the resource before writing the finding.

sections.heading_text: Change one thing and predict the output

That origin begins with an allowed one, so the server sends it back with credentials allowed, and anyone can register a host of that shape. sections.heading: Controls
sections.html:
Standard backed by a cited specification. Baseline this project's default, with reasoning above. Option valid depending on the threat model.

  • StandardThe CORS check reads Access-Control-Allow-Origin, fails if it is absent, succeeds on * only when credentials were not included, otherwise requires it to equal the request's byte-serialised origin, and when credentials were included additionally requires Access-Control-Allow-Credentials to be true. Fetch Standard section 4.10.
  • StandardAccess-Control-Allow-Credentials = %s"true" ; case-sensitive. True does not satisfy it. Fetch Standard section 3.3.4.
  • StandardWith credentials mode include, Access-Control-Allow-Origin cannot be *, and Access-Control-Expose-Headers, Access-Control-Allow-Methods and Access-Control-Allow-Headers can only use * when credentials mode is not include. Fetch Standard section 3.3.5.
  • StandardA serialised origin has no trailing slash, its scheme and domain are lower case ASCII without percent encoding, and this definition "supplants the definition in The Web Origin Concept". Fetch Standard section 3.2, and the table in section 3.3.5 for the trailing slash.
  • StandardAuthorization is the CORS non-wildcard request-header name, so Access-Control-Allow-Headers: * does not cover it, and a cached preflight entry stored as * does not match it. Fetch Standard sections 2.2.2, 4.8 and 4.9.
  • StandardA request avoids a preflight only for a CORS-safelisted method, GET, HEAD or POST, with every header CORS-safelisted: no single safelisted value over 128 bytes, and the safelisted values together not over 1024 bytes. Fetch Standard sections 2.2.1 and 2.2.2 for the definitions, and 4.1 for the preflight condition.
  • StandardA safelisted Content-Type must parse to application/x-www-form-urlencoded, multipart/form-data or text/plain, judged per header rather than through a forgiving extractor, so a server that reads a different duplicate than the browser judged is the hazard the standard warns about. Fetch Standard section 2.2.2.
  • StandardA successful response to a preflight is restricted to an ok status; Access-Control-Max-Age is 5 seconds by default, and a value greater than an imposed limit is set to that limit. Fetch Standard sections 3.3.3 and 4.8.
  • StandardFour non-safelisted Content-Type values are exempted from preflighting by other specifications: application/csp-report, application/expect-ct-report+json, application/xss-auditor-report and application/ocsp-request. Fetch Standard section 3.3.7.
  • StandardThe standard's informative background section says Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * is safe for a resource that could already be fetched by any device on the web, and that using CORS is unsafe for one protected by IP authentication or a firewall. Fetch Standard, Basic safe CORS protocol setup, under Background reading.
  • BaselineHold an allowlist of exact serialised origins and compare byte for byte. Send the matched origin, or no Access-Control-Allow-Origin header at all.
  • BaselineNever construct the header from the request. Reflecting an unchecked origin allows every origin.
  • BaselineSend Vary: Origin on every response whose headers depend on the request's origin.
  • BaselineSet Access-Control-Max-Age deliberately, knowing the browser ceiling, and treat it as the delay before a tightened policy takes effect.
  • BaselineAssert the CORS response headers in tests, against allowed, disallowed and lookalike origins, rather than confirming the integration works in a browser console.
  • BaselineProtect state-changing endpoints with anti-forgery tokens and SameSite cookies. CORS does not stop the request arriving.
  • OptionServe the browser-facing API from the same origin through a reverse proxy, which removes the cross-origin question rather than configuring it.
  • OptionUse a bearer token in Authorization rather than a cookie, so a cross-origin request carries no credential unless the page deliberately attaches one. Name the header in the preflight response.

sections.heading: Review checklist items
sections.html:
These are collected into the site checklist.

  • The allowed origin is never taken from the request Test a disallowed origin and a lookalike such as an allowed host with an extra suffix. Both must come back with no Access-Control-Allow-Origin header.
  • State-changing endpoints are protected independently of CORS A safelisted cross-origin POST is sent with no preflight and the server does the work. Anti-forgery tokens and SameSite cookies are what stop it.
  • Origin comparison is on the serialised form Byte for byte, no trailing slash, scheme and port included. Test the same host over http and with a trailing slash.
  • Vary: Origin is sent wherever the response depends on the origin Otherwise a shared cache can serve one origin's allowed response to another.
  • The Origin header is never used as an authorisation decision A non-browser client sets it freely. It is attacker input outside a browser.
  • Access-Control-Max-Age is set deliberately and bounded It defaults to 5 seconds and browsers clamp it. The value is how long a tightened policy keeps being ignored.
  • Preflight responses are asserted in tests, not confirmed by hand Include a method the endpoint does not support, a request carrying Authorization, and a preflight answered with a redirect.

checks.title: The allowed origin is never taken from the request
checks.detail: Test a disallowed origin and a lookalike such as an allowed host with an extra suffix. Both must come back with no Access-Control-Allow-Origin header.

checks.title: State-changing endpoints are protected independently of CORS
checks.detail: A safelisted cross-origin POST is sent with no preflight and the server does the work. Anti-forgery tokens and SameSite cookies are what stop it.

checks.title: Origin comparison is on the serialised form
checks.detail: Byte for byte, no trailing slash, scheme and port included. Test the same host over http and with a trailing slash.

checks.title: Vary: Origin is sent wherever the response depends on the origin
checks.detail: Otherwise a shared cache can serve one origin's allowed response to another.

checks.title: The Origin header is never used as an authorisation decision

checks.title: Access-Control-Max-Age is set deliberately and bounded
checks.detail: It defaults to 5 seconds and browsers clamp it. The value is how long a tightened policy keeps being ignored.

details.summary: Your API echoes the Origin header back in Access-Control-Allow-Origin and sets Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true. Which origins can read the response?
details.html:
Your API echoes the Origin header back in Access-Control-Allow-Origin and sets Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true. Which origins can read the response?

All of them. The CORS check compares the header against the request's own origin, so echoing makes step 4 compare a value with itself and it can never fail. The configuration is equivalent to publishing every authenticated response to any site a logged-in user happens to visit.

details.summary: A cross-origin POST was blocked by CORS. Did the server process it?
details.html:
A cross-origin POST was blocked by CORS. Did the server process it?

Almost certainly yes. If the content type was safelisted there was no preflight, so the request went straight out, the cookie went with it, and the server did the work. The browser then refused to hand the response to the page. What CORS blocked was the reading, not the writing. Use anti-forgery tokens and SameSite cookies for the writing.

details.summary: You add a bearer token to a working cross-origin integration and it starts failing the preflight, even though the server answers Access-Control-Allow-Headers: *. Why?
details.html:
You add a bearer token to a working cross-origin integration and it starts failing the preflight, even though the server answers Access-Control-Allow-Headers: *. Why?

Authorization is the one CORS non-wildcard request-header name, so * does not cover it. The server has to name it. The same rule applies to the preflight cache, so an entry previously stored as * will not match it either.

Is Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * a finding?

Only with context. For data that anyone could already fetch with curl, it is the correct header and the standard says so. It is unsafe in exactly one shape: when the resource is protected by where the caller is rather than by who they are, such as an IP allowlist or a firewall, because then a browser inside the perimeter becomes the route in. Ask what protects the resource before writing the finding.

Every option, and why
  • Check 66 still prints failure. https://booking-rewards.example does not begin with either listed origin, so a prefix test refuses it too. An unrelated origin is the test a loosened comparison still passes.
  • The lab carries a lookalike origin for exactly this edit, so the run does not stay clean. It exits 1.
  • Correct. Exit 1, two failures. Check 70 goes from ['success', 'success', 'failure', 'failure', 'failure'] to ['success', 'success', 'failure', 'success', 'failure'], and in check 71 the fourth entry goes from None to 'https://app.examplehotels.example.evil.example'. That origin begins with an allowed one, so the server sends it back with credentials allowed, and anyone can register a host of that shape. Checks 65 to 68 print the same as before, which is why check cors-01 in the Reference layer asks for a lookalike as well as a disallowed origin.
  • The fifth origin is http://app.examplehotels.example. It differs from the listed origin inside the scheme, before the host starts, so it is not a prefix match and its entry in checks 70 and 71 does not move.

Every option, and why
  • A wildcard succeeds only when credentials were not included. Checks 62, 63 and 69 all call cors_check with "include", so the wildcard line is skipped and * is then compared with the origin as a plain string. It equals none of them.
  • The check has no idea which origin is the real app. It compares one string with another, and * differs from https://app.examplehotels.example just as it differs from the attacker's origin.
  • Check 69 runs against reflecting_server, which has no list. ALLOWED_ORIGINS is read only by allowlist_server, and check 70 is the one that uses it.

The edit closes the hole by breaking the integration, which is not a fix anyone keeps. Check cors-02 in the Reference layer is the assertion that catches this pairing before it ships.

  • Not in this lab. Check 44 sends its request with credentials included, and the loop that is left honours * in Access-Control-Allow-Headers only when credentials are not included. Authorization is an unsafe name that was not listed, so the preflight is still refused.

The allowed response is the one that names an origin and allows credentials, so it is the one a shared cache must not serve to a different origin, and it is now the one with nothing telling the cache so.
